title: Value investing (concept)

overview.objective: Buy shares for less than a careful estimate of what the business is worth.
overview.context: A concept page. Value investing rests on estimates of a business's worth, and those estimates can be wrong.

simple.simple: [[value-investing|Value investing]] means estimating what a company is worth, then buying only when the price is well below that estimate. The gap is the [[margin-of-safety]].
simple.balanced: The estimate depends on assumptions about future cash flows, so two careful people can disagree widely. A share can look cheap because the business is shrinking: a [[value-trap]]. Cheap shares can stay cheap for years, and checking [[free-cash-flow]] and debt is part of the work, not optional.

reasoning: If the market sometimes prices a business below what its future cash flows are worth, buying at a discount could leave room for error and for the price to recover. That is the reasoning; markets may have good reasons for the low price.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional company? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional company. The share price is 30 and earnings per share are 3. Free cash flow has been negative for 3 years and debt is rising. Your estimate of its worth is 45.

options.text: The margin of safety on your estimate is about 33%
Negative free cash flow and rising debt are warning signs of a possible value trap
options.explanation: Right: profits that do not turn into cash deserve a closer look.

options.text: The P/E of 10 is below the estimate's implied P/E of 12
The estimate of 45 is a fact
options.explanation: No: it is an estimate built on assumptions.

failureAnalysis: The business keeps shrinking, so the cheap price was justified.
The estimate of worth was too optimistic.
The price stays low for years, tying up money.
Debt problems wipe out shareholders before any recovery.
limitations: This page explains the idea; it gives no rules to pick shares.
Valuation needs assumptions, and small changes to them move the estimate a lot.
No claim is made that value investing beats other approaches.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: You estimate a business is worth 80 per share. It trades at 60. What is the margin of safety?

options.explanation: No: the margin is measured against the estimated value, not the price.
No: 20 is the gap in money; the margin is usually given as a share of the estimate.
Right: the gap divided by the estimated value.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 5 while similar companies trade at 15. What should you check first?

options.explanation: Right: a low P/E can mean earnings are about to fall.

options.text: Whether the price rose this week
options.explanation: No: last week's price says little about value.

options.text: Nothing more, since a low P/E alone is enough to show it is good value
options.explanation: No: that is how value traps catch people.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does an estimate of a business's worth rely on?

options.explanation: No: value estimates come from the business, not the chart.
Right: and different assumptions give different values.

options.text: A fixed formula that gives the same answer whoever uses it and whatever they assume
options.explanation: No: estimates change with the assumptions.
